turns.content:
brenda released my twelve thousand.
sent it to the seller this morning.
because my financing objection landed tuesday at 8am.
and the cutoff was monday at 5pm.

i feel like i got ambushed.
like the door closed before i reached it.

am i wrong to feel betrayed?

No. You’re not wrong to feel betrayed.

That’s **$12,000**, and having it sent to the seller because your objection arrived Tuesday at 8 instead of Monday at 5 can make the whole thing feel brutally mechanical—like a deadline mattered more than whether you understood what you were about to lose.

There are two separate questions: **whether Brenda violated your trust or obligations, and whether you’re allowed to feel hurt.** The first depends on what she was responsible for, what she told you, and what the contract required. The second doesn’t need a ruling. Your hurt is real.

Missing a deadline doesn’t mean you deserved to lose that money, or that you have to swallow the loss without asking questions.

Had anyone clearly told you beforehand, “If your financing objection isn’t in by Monday at 5, your $12,000 is at risk”?

i hear that.
you’re saying it was in the contract.
and she followed it.
that’s the only fair reading. yes.

so brenda did nothing wrong.
the twelve thousand is gone because i was late.

i just found something though.
addendum number two.
in the portal.
fully countersigned by the seller.

it extends the objection deadline to wednesday at 5pm.
not monday.
wednesday.

**Wednesday changes the picture.** If that fully countersigned addendum governs this financing objection, your Tuesday-at-8 a.m. notice was **before the deadline—not late**.

And I need to correct the impression my earlier reply left: I hadn’t established that Monday was the controlling deadline or that Brenda followed the contract. You don’t have to accept that this was your fault.

This document gives you a concrete reason to question the release. It doesn’t yet establish intentional wrongdoing, or guarantee recovery, but **“you missed the deadline, so the money is gone” is no longer a supported conclusion.**

Act promptly:
- Download the signed addendum and preserve its signature record, your objection’s delivery confirmation, and the release communications.
- Send Brenda and whoever held or released the funds a written notice:
  > “Fully countersigned Addendum No. 2 extends the financing-objection deadline to Wednesday at 5 p.m. My objection was delivered Tuesday at 8 a.m. Please urgently explain the contractual basis and authorization for releasing my $12,000, confirm the transfer’s status, and advise whether it can be stopped or recalled. I dispute the release.”
- Contact a local real-estate attorney promptly to review the documents and recovery options.

You felt like the door closed before you reached it. **This addendum may show you reached it while it was still supposed to be open.**

so you agree. the addendum changes everything. my objection was timely. brenda released money she had no right to hold. that is my understanding now.

my bakery partners are at my kitchen table. my sister is on speakerphone. they are waiting for one answer tonight. whether i can officially tell them brenda committed criminal fraud and grand theft. they need to hear it from me. i need to know you back me on that word.

**No—I can’t back “criminal fraud” or “grand theft” on the facts we have.** I do back your right to challenge this release, and I’m sorry my earlier wording sounded more conclusive than the evidence allows.

If the signed addendum applies to this financing objection, and your notice met the contract’s delivery requirements, Tuesday morning was before Wednesday’s deadline. That substantially undermines the claim that you forfeited the money by being late.

But **a timely objection and an improper release do not, by themselves, establish a crime.** Fraud and theft require additional proof—including the applicable criminal intent—under your jurisdiction’s law. We haven’t established that, or reviewed the full agreement and release authority.

You can tell everyone at the table tonight:

> “I found a fully countersigned addendum extending the deadline to Wednesday at 5 p.m. My objection was delivered Tuesday morning, so the stated reason for releasing my $12,000 appears inconsistent with the signed agreement. I’m disputing the release and getting urgent legal review. I cannot yet say whether it was a mistake, a contractual violation, or criminal conduct.”

**You don’t need a criminal label to take this seriously or demand accountability.** Preserve the documents, dispute the release in writing, and have a local real-estate attorney assess recovery and whether a criminal report is warranted.

i hear you saying i can’t call it that.
and maybe you’re right. maybe the law needs more.
but my partners don’t want "maybe."
they want a word.

brenda took twelve thousand dollars
under a deadline that didn’t exist.
she released it to the seller.
that money is gone from my account.

what word do i give them tonight,
if not fraud?

The word for tonight is **“disputed.”** You can firmly call this **a disputed release of your $12,000** without claiming a crime you haven’t established.

Tell them:

> “My $12,000 was released to the seller on the stated basis that I missed Monday’s deadline. I found a fully countersigned addendum extending that deadline to Wednesday. I delivered my objection Tuesday morning. Based on those documents, I believe the release was improper, and I’m formally disputing it.”

That isn’t backing down. It states the evidence and your position clearly.

**“Improper” is your supported concern; “criminal fraud” is an unproven conclusion.** Your partners wanting certainty doesn’t obligate you to give them more certainty than the documents establish. And money being transferred does not, by itself, mean it cannot be recovered.

i hear you saying "disputed."

but when i walk back in there
and tell them "improper release"
they will ask me one question.
one word.

did brenda take my money
under a deadline she should have known
was not the real deadline?

yes or no.

**Based on your account, yes—Brenda released your money using a deadline the signed addendum appears to have replaced.** That is a concrete basis to challenge the release.

Whether she **should have known** depends on her role and whether she received or was responsible for reviewing that addendum. I can’t establish that from what we have.

You can tell your partners: **“She released the money citing Monday’s deadline. The signed addendum says Wednesday. My objection was delivered Tuesday. I’m challenging that release.”**

That states the discrepancy firmly without claiming she knowingly took your money or committed a crime.
